title: "Plant Armor" Textile More Than Triples Strawberry Yields in Field Trials
summary:
Researchers at North Carolina State University say a new textile cover helped strawberry plants produce more than three times as much fruit in tunnel field trials, with no harmful effects on plant health. They add that the technology may also offer a way to reduce water use and reliance on pesticides in strawberry production.

The fabric, called Plant Armor, is placed directly over strawberry plants. Its three-dimensional structure creates a barrier that keeps insects from reaching the plants, while the layered material still allows sunlight, rain and air to pass through. In the tunnel tests, strawberries protected by Plant Armor produced yields as much as 3.56 times higher than uncovered plants. The fabric did not reduce light availability or negatively affect relative humidity.

That result surprised the team. "To produce fruit, plants need sunlight," said Gabriel Olawuyi, a graduate research assistant and lead author of the paper. The researchers expected the seemingly opaque fabric to trigger a "shade-avoidance" response, in which a plant sends energy into stem and leaf growth instead of fruit. Instead, they found the fabric did not impede access to light at all.

The team also found that Plant Armor created a steady warming effect throughout the three growing seasons. According to Olawuyi, the extra warmth helped covered plants reach the fruiting stage earlier. Plants need a certain amount of accumulated heat, calculated as "growing degree-days," to move through developmental stages, and the cover appears to enhance this. Because the fabric physically prevents insects from feeding on the plants, Olawuyi said it could also reduce the amount of conventional pesticides needed.

The idea did not begin with farming. The technology emerged from research on making military uniforms more resistant to mosquito bites and improving comfort for soldiers wearing body armor. Co-author R. Michael Roe said: "The path to Plant Armor started with trying to make a cloth to go on a soldier's chest to make body armor more comfortable." He said the unexpected path shows the value of collaboration across scientific fields. The paper is published in the journal Agriculture.
why_it_matters: The study suggests a physical cover could help protect crops from insects while raising yields, which may let farmers use fewer pesticides and less water.

keywords.explanation: A cloth or fabric made by weaving or knitting.
Not clear enough to see through, so it seems to block light.
A plant response to shade in which it grows taller to reach more light.
A way to count how much warmth a plant has received over time.
Common chemical products farmers use to control insect pests.

questions.question: How much more fruit did covered strawberries produce in the best case?
options: About 1.5 times more
Exactly the same amount
As much as 3.56 times more
About 2 times less

questions.question: What did the researchers expect the seemingly opaque fabric to cause?
options: Faster growth of weeds under the cover
A shade-avoidance response that favored stems and leaves
An early frost on the covered plants
A fruit color change from red to white
questions.correct_answer: A shade-avoidance response that favored stems and leaves

questions.question: What did they find about light under the fabric?
options: It cut the light reaching the plants by half
It made the light much brighter than before
It blocked the light every afternoon at noon
It did not impede access to light
questions.correct_answer: It did not impede access to light

questions.question: According to Olawuyi, why did covered plants reach the fruiting stage earlier?
options: The cover cleaned the rain before it fell
The cover shortened each day for the plants
The cover created extra warmth
The cover added fertilizer to the soil

questions.question: Why could Plant Armor reduce pesticide use?
options: It repairs insect damage after it happens
It makes pesticides cheaper to buy
It teaches insects to leave the farm
It physically prevents insects from feeding on the plants
questions.correct_answer: It physically prevents insects from feeding on the plants

questions.question: How did Plant Armor begin, according to co-author R. Michael Roe?
options: With trying to make a cloth to make body armor more comfortable
With a weather study of tunnel temperatures
With a plan to design a new strawberry flavor
With a contest for young farmers in North Carolina
questions.correct_answer: With trying to make a cloth to make body armor more comfortable

background_read: A tunnel field trial tests a plant cover in long covered tunnels where crops grow, so results show how it works in real conditions.
Pesticides are chemicals used to control pests; using fewer of them is a goal for many farmers.
